text: Hello, my name is Paromita Sengupta. title: Do heavier penguins have longer flippers? An R analysis
text:
Penguins on the Palmer Archipelago come in three species that look quite different in size. In this post I use R to ask two simple questions:

How does body mass differ between the three species?
Within a species, do penguins with longer flippers weigh more?

Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The data ship inside the palmerpenguins R package, so nothing is downloaded when this page is built. The data are released under the CC0 licence.
Citation: Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. R package version 0.1.0. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3960218. The measurements were collected by Gorman KB, Williams TD, Fraser WR (2014), PLoS ONE 9(3): e90081.

  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_mass = round(mean(body_mass_g)),
    sd_mass = round(sd(body_mass_g)),
    min_mass = min(body_mass_g),
    max_mass = max(body_mass_g)

title: Do heavier penguins have longer flippers? An R analysis
text:
Flipper length and body mass

ggplot(penguins_clean,
       aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 2: Flipper length against body mass. Each species has its own fitted line.





To put a number on the trend, I fit a linear model of body mass on flipper length, with species as an additional predictor.

model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species, data = penguins_clean)
kable(round(summary(model)$coefficients, 2))

title: Do heavier penguins have longer flippers? An R analysis
text:
What I found

Gentoo penguins are clearly heavier than the other two species.
Within the data, longer flippers go with heavier birds. The model estimates about 40.7 g more body mass for each extra millimetre of flipper, holding species fixed.
This is an observational association. It says nothing about whether flipper length causes weight.

title: Bill length and depth in penguins: a Python analysis
text:
In my R post I looked at body mass and flipper length. Here I use Python on the same dataset to ask a different question: Is a penguin’s bill length related to its bill depth? The answer turns out to depend on whether you look at all penguins together or one species at a time.

title: Bill length and depth in penguins: a Python analysis
text:
Pooled trend versus within-species trend
First, the correlation across all penguins together. Then, the correlation inside each species.

overall_r = penguins_clean["bill_length_mm"].corr(penguins_clean["bill_depth_mm"])

within_r = (
    penguins_clean.groupby("species")[bill_cols]
    .apply(lambda g: g["bill_length_mm"].corr(g["bill_depth_mm"]))
    .rename("correlation")
)

print(f"All penguins pooled: r = {overall_r:.2f}")
within_r.round(2).to_frame()

y_all = penguins_clean["bill_depth_mm"]

ax1.scatter(x_all, y_all, alpha=0.6, color="grey")
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x_all, y_all, 1)
xs = np.linspace(x_all.min(), x_all.max(), 100)
ax1.plot(xs, slope * xs + intercept, color="black")
ax1.set_title("All penguins pooled")

for name, group in penguins_clean.groupby("species"):
    ax2.scatter(group["bill_length_mm"], group["bill_depth_mm"], label=name, alpha=0.6)
    s, i = np.polyfit(group["bill_length_mm"], group["bill_depth_mm"], 1)
    xs = np.linspace(group["bill_length_mm"].min(), group["bill_length_mm"].max(), 50)
    ax2.plot(xs, s * xs + i)
ax2.set_title("Split by species")
ax2.legend(title="Species")

plt.tight_layout()

Figure 1: Bill length against bill depth. Left: all penguins with one pooled trend line. Right: the same points with one trend line per species.

title: Bill length and depth in penguins: a Python analysis
text:
What I found

Across all penguins pooled, bill length and bill depth are negatively correlated (r = np.float64(-0.24)). Figure 1 shows this in the left panel.
Within each species the relationship reverses. The correlations range from np.float64(0.39) to np.float64(0.65), all positive.
The pooled trend is misleading because species differ in both measurements: Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills, and Adelie penguins have short but deep ones. This is an example of Simpson’s paradox, and it is a good reason to look at group structure before trusting a pooled correlation.
